Empirical Research Plan  
“Scars of War: The Long-Run Economic Consequences of WWII Bombing on Japanese Cities”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with continuous treatment intensity, complemented by an event–study (Sun & Abraham, 2021) specification.  

Why appropriate  
•  Treatment (bombing intensity in 1944-45) is a one-off, plausibly exogenous shock.  
•  We observe multiple pretreatment years (1920, 1930, 1936, 1940) and many post-war waves (1950-1970-1980-1990).  
•  City and year fixed effects purge time-invariant city characteristics and common aggregate shocks.  
•  The event-study allows visual and statistical testing of the parallel-trend assumption and of dynamic adjustment paths.  

Supplementary strategy (robustness):  
•  Instrumental‐variables DID where actual destruction is instrumented with “pre-announced target priority” (binary variable = 1 if the city appears on U.S. 20th Air Force target lists as of mid-1944).  
•  Synthetic-control case studies for the largest, very rare events (Tokyo, Hiroshima, Nagasaki).

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
BombDestructionᵢ = share of built‐up area destroyed (0-1) OR tons of bombs per km².  
•  “High-damage” cities = BombDestruction ≥ 0.25 (robustness: alt. cut-offs, continuous).

Control group  
Cities with BombDestruction < 0.05 (essentially unbombed). These cities provide the counterfactual evolution absent large-scale destruction.

Treatment timing  
Treatment occurs between March 1944 and August 1945 (coded as event year 0).  
Pretreatment years: ≤ 1940.  
Post-treatment: ≥ 1950.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1 (Parallel trends)  
Absent bombing, treated and control cities would have followed the same path.  
Plausibility: U.S. targeting doctrine emphasized military value, shipping lanes, and weather windows, not growth prospects. Will test in event-study using 1920-1940 trends.

A2 (No differential time‐varying shocks)  
No other shock differentially hit treated cities after 1945 (e.g., differential Reconstruction Aid).  
Plausibility: Japanese central government allocated reconstruction funds according to damage, but we can control for these transfers.

A3 (SUTVA / no cross-city spillovers)  
Destruction in city i does not directly change outcomes in city j (except through displaced population, which is a channel, not a violation, if counted in j’s outcome).  
Plausibility: Some migration spillovers likely; we will test for them by excluding nearest-neighbor cities or using prefecture-level population totals.

A4 (Measurement validity)  
Bombing data accurately measure destruction intensity.  
Plausibility: U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey provides precise maps; measurement error likely classical.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1 Non-random targeting of larger / industrial cities  
•  Mitigation: control flexibly for pre-war population, industrial share, and growth trend.  
•  Propensity-score re-weighting to balance pre-war observables.  
•  IV approach using U.S. “target priority” list as instrument.

T2 Post-war reconstruction aid endogenous to bombing  
•  Collect city-level reconstruction spending, include it as a control or use it as an outcome to document mechanism.  
•  Show results robust to excluding the 5% most-aided cities.

T3 Migration spillovers distort control outcomes  
•  Run regressions on prefecture-population totals (bombed + unbombed cities) so migration within prefecture nets to zero.  
•  Exclude nearest 50 km neighbors of treated cities in robustness checks.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast FE & IV regressions
library(modelsummary) # neat tables
library(did)          # Callaway & Sant’Anna, event study alt.
library(haven)        # if Stata dta files appear later

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data (assume one CSV)
# -------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("japan_city_bombing_panel.csv")

# Key variables assumed in raw data:
# city_id, year, population, gdp_pc, bombs_tons, area_km2,
# prewar_pop_1940, target_priority (0/1), recon_spend

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct variables
# -------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(bomb_intensity = bombs_tons / area_km2,
         treated       = (bomb_intensity >= 0.25),             # baseline dummy
         post          = (year >= 1950),
         ln_pop        = log(population),
         ln_gdp_pc     = log(gdp_pc),
         event_time    = year - 1945)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID specification
# ln(Y_ict) = α_i + γ_t + β * (treated_i * post_t) + X_i + ε
# -------------------------------------------------
did_pop <- feols(ln_pop ~ treated:post + prewar_pop_1940 + i(year) | city_id + year,
                 data = df, cluster = "city_id")

did_gdp <- feols(ln_gdp_pc ~ treated:post + prewar_pop_1940 + i(year) | city_id + year,
                 data = df, cluster = "city_id")

modelsummary(list(did_pop, did_gdp), stars = TRUE)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham)
# -------------------------------------------------
es <- feols(ln_pop ~ sunab(treated, event_time) | city_id + year,
            cluster = "city_id", data = df)

iplot(es)  # pre-trend & dynamic effect plot

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. IV robustness (target_priority as Z)
# -------------------------------------------------
iv_did <- feols(ln_pop ~ 1 | city_id + year | 
                  I(bomb_intensity) ~ target_priority, 
                data = df %>% filter(post == TRUE),
                cluster = "city_id")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 6. Spillover robustness: drop neighbors within 50km
# -------------------------------------------------
df_nospill <- df %>% filter(nearest_bombed_city_km > 50)
did_nospill <- feols(ln_pop ~ treated:post | city_id + year,
                     data = df_nospill, cluster = "city_id")
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory (Duranton & Puga; urban recovery literature) predicts heavy short-run destruction lowers population and economic activity sharply, but agglomeration forces promote partial rebound.

Prior:  
•  Immediate post-war (1950): a city that lost 50 % of its built area records ≈ 30 % lower population relative to trend.  
•  By 1970: gap shrinks to ≈ 5-10 %.  
•  GDP per capita may recover faster than population (capital deepening in reconstruction phase).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
Criterion (1 = satisfied, 0 = weak)  
1. Plausible exogeneity of treatment ………………… 0.8  
2. Parallel pretreatment trends ………………………… 1.0 (testable)  
3. No major spillovers/SUTVA …………………………… 0.5  
4. Accurate measurement of key vars ………………… 0.9  
5. Robustness across specifications …………………… 0.9  

Overall: 4.1 / 5 → Good but not perfect; main weakness is potential spatial spillovers.
